About this citation

Published after Wittgenstein's death from material he had reworked repeatedly. The first part is a numbered sequence of remarks; the second part is a later addition and its status is disputed. The archive cites § numbers, which is the standard reference.

Exact wording

English (as recorded here)
“Don’t think, but look!”
German
“Denk nicht, sondern schau!”

Philosophical Investigations §66, in the discussion of games and family resemblance. English “Don’t think, but look!” is the standard Anscombe/Rhees rendering.

Forms in circulation that differ

  • “Don’t think, but look!”
  • “Don't think, look!”

Attribution notes

Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §66. Imperative addressed to someone tempted to assume a single essence of “game.” Quoting it as a general anti-intellectual motto detaches it from the method of looking at cases that the section teaches.

About Ludwig Wittgenstein

Ludwig Wittgenstein (1889–1951), born in Vienna to a wealthy industrial family, studied engineering then logic with Russell at Cambridge. The Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921) aimed to draw limits to sense; he then left academic philosophy for years as a teacher and architect’s assistant.

Interpretation

Wittgenstein is giving a method, not an anti-intellectual slogan. In the Investigations he argues that philosophical problems arise when we theorise about how language must work instead of looking at how it is actually used. "Don't think, but look!" instructs the reader to replace speculation with description of real cases. The point is that the confusion is generated by the theory, so more theory deepens it.

Why it matters

It transfers well beyond philosophy: when a question will not resolve, check whether it was generated by a model rather than by anything observed. If so, the way forward is usually to describe the cases first.

Questions readers arrive with

What is the source of the quotation “Don’t think, but look!”?

“Don’t think, but look!” comes from Philosophical Investigations, §66 (1953 (posthumous)), attributed to Ludwig Wittgenstein.

What does Ludwig Wittgenstein mean by language?

Across 4 recurring voices here (notably Ludwig Wittgenstein and Kwasi Wiredu), language is framed through Analytic Philosophy and Africana Philosophy. Some passages define language; others warn how it fails; still others relocate it inside habit, community, or language. This passage enters that discussion through language, method.

Is the wording of this Ludwig Wittgenstein quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “Don’t think, but look!” Forms in circulation that differ: Don’t think, but look! / Don't think, look! The German reads “Denk nicht, sondern schau!”

Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §66. Imperative addressed to someone tempted to assume a single essence of “game.” Quoting it as a general anti-intellectual motto detaches it from the method of looking at cases that the section teaches.
